1.pericope_label: The altar of burnt offering; its horns, vessels and grating

schools.summary: Resolve the conflict with the earlier altar law by making this a bronze-plated case filled with earth at each halt; deny that horned altars were common outside Israel; trace the horns from ornament to essential; and refuse to decide where the grating stood.

Answer the same question about horns from numismatic evidence for horned heathen altars; reconstruct the altar and grating from Calmet while admitting the variety of opinion; and compute the dimensions in feet and inches.

Rule out the usual devotional identifications of the altar — the heart, the communion table — and build the type instead on the burnt offering’s name, which means mounting upward, and on the Spirit as the fire by which flesh is made an acceptable victim.
Place the altar in the court as the meeting-point of a settled communion, where the people bring what the priests offer and the altar sanctifies the gift.

debates: Whether horns were peculiar to Israelite altars (Ellicott, against Kalisch) or common among the heathen (Clarke, from coin reverses).

Where the grating stood: from mid-altar down, shielding the sides from the priests’ feet, or around the top, catching fallen pieces — Ellicott says the data cannot decide; Wesley, Clarke and Gill each reconstruct it differently.
How an altar of wood stands with the command that altars be of earth or unhewn stone — Ellicott and Keil both answer that the wood was only a case for earth.
What the altar typifies: not the heart and not the Lord’s table (Gill, explicitly), but the offering of flesh through the Spirit (Calvin).
outliers: Clarke alone adduces Roman coinage as evidence about altar design.
Gill alone spends his comment ruling out identifications rather than proposing one.
Ellicott alone explains the avoidance of curved lines in Hebrew furniture as a matter of difficulty rather than doctrine.

schools.summary: Insist the altar was genuinely hollow and reject the rabbinic reconstruction that fills it with earth; make the hollowness a figure of Christ’s self-emptying; and give the grate and the altar separate sets of rings.
Take the altar for a framework with nothing solid inside, covered only by the grating, and explain the arrangement by portability.
Report the carrying arrangements as the text gives them, and refer back rather than repeat.

debates: Whether the hollow was left empty (Gill, Clarke) or filled with earth at each halt (the Targum of Jonathan and other Jewish writers, reported and rejected by Gill; assumed by Keil and by Ellicott earlier in the chapter). The two readings are incompatible and the chapter’s commentators are evenly split.

Whether the staves passed through the rings of the grate (Jarchi), through rings projecting from the frame so as to bind grate and altar together (Lightfoot, reported by Gill), or through rings belonging to the altar alone (Gill’s own view).
outliers: Gill alone reads the hollowness of the altar as a figure of the self-emptying of Christ.

9.pericope_label: The court of the tabernacle; its hangings, pillars and sockets

schools.summary: Read the court as the church, its pillars its stability and its linen the righteousness of saints, and rejoice that the enclosure is now taken down so that men may pray everywhere.

Read the same enclosure as the visible church, mixed of saints and hypocrites because every sort of Israelite entered it; take the pillars for gospel ministers; and find in the people’s exclusion from the sanctuary both the condition of mankind and the assurance that unworthy outcasts are received.

Correct the renderings — sail-cloth rather than hangings, multi-strand thread rather than fine linen, connecting-rods rather than fillets — argue against a modern that the pillars were bronze, and defend the eastward orientation against any charge of sun-worship.
Compute the court’s dimensions and note that its low walls left the tabernacle visible from outside.

debates: What the court typifies: the church of the righteous, whose enclosure the gospel has removed (Henry, Wesley), or the visible church containing saints and hypocrites together (Gill).
What the pillars were made of: cedar (Philo), shittim wood (most), or bronze like their sockets (Gill, with Josephus and the plain text) — while Ellicott has to argue the same point against Kalisch.
Whether the hangings were opaque or open enough to see through — Ellicott argues from the rare word for a woven sail-cloth that the court was visible within.
outliers: Ellicott alone anticipates the charge that an eastward-facing sanctuary implies sun-worship, and denies it.
Gill alone reasons from the number of pillars to the spacing between them.
Wesley’s comment here is Henry’s, reproduced almost entire.

16.pericope_label: The gate of the court; the pillars filleted; all the vessels of brass

schools.summary: Identify the gate hanging with the covering of the dwelling’s entrance and note how its colour marked the way in; correct filleted to united by rods; observe that every measurement of the structure is five cubits or a multiple; take the brass vessels for erection tools; and trace the court itself to the nation’s exclusion from immediate access.

Explain the repetition of the silver fillets as covering the two ends omitted earlier, and prefer the erection-tools reading of the brass vessels on the ground that sanctuary vessels were gold or silver.
Match the gate hanging to the tabernacle’s coverings and veils, and read the brass vessels as altar instruments, the cheaper metal chosen because precious ones would soon be worn out by hard service.

debates: What the brass vessels were: the tools for pitching and striking the tabernacle (Keil, and Gill after weighing both) or the instruments used about the altar (Clarke).

Why brass rather than a precious metal: because true sanctuary vessels were gold or silver, so these must be something else (Gill), or because precious metal would not have survived the service (Clarke).
Why the silver fillets are specified a second time — answered only by Gill, and as a matter of drafting rather than of substance.
outliers: Ellicott alone notices that every measurement of the tabernacle and court, as against its furniture, is five cubits or a multiple, and names the single exception.

20.pericope_label: The pure beaten oil; the lamps ordered from evening to morning

schools.summary: Take the lamps as burning day and night; read the pure oil as the graces of the Spirit received from Christ the good olive; draw the maintenance of ministers from the people’s providing it; and make the tending of the lamps the ministry of the word.

Restrict the burning to the hours of darkness against Josephus, arguing both from the daylight the curtain admitted and from the texts on lighting and extinction; specify what beaten oil was and note the new particularity of the requirement; and take the tent’s name from God’s meeting with his people.

Agree that the lamps were extinguished by morning, describe the mother drop from a Roman authority on husbandry, extend the emblem to the devotion of true worshippers, and derive the tent’s name from the assembling of the congregation.

Rest on the purity of the oil rather than its substance, since any fault would have detracted from the dignity of the mystery; and press the perpetual flame, since it is not enough to be enlightened by puffs.

debates: Whether the lamps burned continually or only from evening to morning: day and night (Henry, Wesley), night only (Ellicott, Clarke, Keil), or three of the seven kept alight by day (Josephus, reported and rejected by both Ellicott and Clarke).

Why the tent is called the tabernacle of the congregation: because Israel assembled there (Clarke), because God met Moses there (Keil, Ellicott), or — Gill, rejecting both — because Israel assembled at its door and God met them there.
Whether the daylight entering through the linen curtain made lamps unnecessary by day, which Ellicott makes an argument and no one else raises.
outliers: Gill alone declares the usual explanations of the sanctuary’s name untenable and offers a third.
Clarke alone cites a Roman writer on husbandry for the quality of unpressed oil, and alone suggests the perpetual fire of Vesta was modelled on this rite.
Calvin alone insists that intermittent illumination is no illumination — that it is not enough to be enlightened by puffs.
